newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-HK graft-buster vows no let-up under China.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK graft-buster vows no let-up under China.

text.p: It has swooped on crooked officials, a passport-peddling U.S. consular officer, ruthless triad gangsters, and bribe-taking police.
Set up in 1974 after a corrupt police chief fled Hong Kong, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) has earned a reputation as a fearless warrior on graft.
The operative word is "independent" -- its ability to fight graft wherever it occurs hinges on its independence.
The word was inexplicably omitted when Chinese and English-language negotiators drafted a constitutional clause effective for when China takes over the territory on July 1.

"Some people may argue: what is in a word? That happens to be a very important word -- independent -- and, I would say, essential," said ICAC chief Lily Yam, a veteran civil servant who only took the post of commissioner early this year.
The graft-busters have won a promise from Hong Kong's future rulers to retain "independent" in its title after July 1.
But they must still reassure an anxious public that they will be independent in practice, as well as in word.
HOLDING THE LINE AFTER THE HANDOVER
Some sceptics fear the graft-busters may find themselves hobbled after the handover -- particularly if investigations target senior mainland officials.
"The number one concern among our clients is whether Hong Kong can hold the line on corruption, Stephen Vickers, Kroll Associates (Asia) Ltd senior managing director told Reuters.
"Clearly, corruption is endemic in the People's Republic of China despite fairly valiant efforts to have a go at reform," Vickers said.
But Yam said there will be no letup in the ICAC's pursuit of the corrupt after July 1: "We are determined to enforce the law impartially and relentlessly."
She added: "We have every determination to pursue corruption -- whatever his (the suspect's) background, whatever his connections, she said.
HONG KONG ONE OF ASIA'S CLEANEST BUSINESS CENTRES
The ICAC has made Hong Kong one of the cleanest places in Asia to do business, partly because of its tremendous muscle.
"Its powers are immense," author Jan Morris wrote of the ICAC in her book, "Hong Kong".

"It can act without higher authority to inspect any institution, public or private, it can hold suspects without trial indefinitely, and it receives an inexhaustible flow of intelligence about the private lives of everyone, from the governor down."
Such powers were needed in the free-wheeling territory, with the then graft-ridden police feeling the effects.
The ICAC rounded up the police, arresting almost 60 police from one division. One senior superintendent committed suicide, and three British superintendents were taken into custody.
ICAC -- NO RESPECTER OF PERSONS
No one is beyong the agency's reach.
Targets have included a disgraced government lawyer, a corrupt U.S. consular official jailed over bogus passports, and even one of its own, a top ICAC official.
It managed to jail a corrupt Customs officer despite the triad murder of a key witness.
Yam said the anti-graft body plans to get even tougher in its fight in the future, deploying another 40 agents to the frontline and increasing intelligence activities.
It is also liaising with the Guangdong People's Procurate in Guangdong province, which borders Hong Kong.
Despite the ICAC's reputation for toughness, its neighbours across the border take a stronger line.
Those found guilty of graft in China face the death sentence -- a bullet in the head paid for by the offender's family.
But under the "one country-two systems" arrangement such penalties will not apply in mainly-autonomous Hong Kong.
